Minimal change disease: 2

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A biopsy from a patient with minimal change disease appears nearly normal on light microscopy. Electron microscopy is then reviewed to identify the characteristic podocyte abnormality. Which ultrastructural finding is most expected?

  1. Frequent corticosteroid responsiveness in typical childhood disease
  2. Predominantly albumin-rich proteinuria
  3. Podocyte foot-process effacement
  4. Near-normal glomeruli on light microscopy
  5. No substantial immune deposits on immunofluorescence
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Podocyte foot-process effacement

Electron microscopy detects loss of normal podocyte foot-process architecture in many proteinuric diseases.

Understanding the options

Podocyte foot-process effacement
Electron microscopy detects loss of normal podocyte foot-process architecture in many proteinuric diseases.
Near-normal glomeruli on light microscopy
Minimal change disease can have striking proteinuria despite little visible light-microscopic change. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
No substantial immune deposits on immunofluorescence
Classic minimal change disease lacks the immune-complex staining pattern of membranous nephropathy. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Frequent corticosteroid responsiveness in typical childhood disease
Typical childhood minimal change disease often responds to corticosteroids; atypical or resistant cases require reassessment. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
Predominantly albumin-rich proteinuria
Minimal change disease often has relatively selective albumin loss, reflecting altered filtration-barrier function. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
